metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Buffalo, WY | Johnson County
metaDescription: Buffalo, WY is the Johnson County seat on the Powder River Basin's western edge, coalbed methane history and conventional oil both in play here.
heroLead: Buffalo is the Johnson County seat, sitting where the Bighorn Mountains meet the western edge of the Powder River Basin, and the mineral history under this county runs through both a coalbed methane boom and a much older conventional oil story.
intro: Johnson County saw real coalbed methane development during the boom years of the late 1990s and 2000s, when operators targeted shallow coal seams for methane gas across the Powder River Basin, before that play largely went bust as gas prices collapsed and a lot of those wells were plugged or abandoned. Older, deeper conventional production has a longer history in pockets of the county as well.

If your family's interest around Buffalo traces to that CBM era, I want to know whether the wells are still producing, plugged, or somewhere in between, because that status changes everything about what the interest is worth today.

sections.heading: The CBM boom and what came after
paragraphs: Coalbed methane wells produce differently than conventional oil and gas, they often start slow while water is pumped off the coal seam, then ramp up gas production before declining. When prices crashed, a lot of Powder River Basin CBM wells stopped being economic to operate, and many were plugged well before their reserves were fully depleted.

That history means some Johnson County royalty owners saw checks that started, grew, then simply stopped years ago. If that's your situation, your interest still has value, priced on whether the underlying wellbore could realistically be reactivated or re-drilled, not on the current absence of a check.

sections.heading: Older conventional production
paragraphs: Beneath and alongside the CBM-era wells, Johnson County has pockets of older, deeper conventional oil production that predates the coalbed boom entirely. These tend to be lower-volume, longer-lived assets with their own separate lease and royalty history, distinct from the CBM story even on the same or adjacent tracts.

sections.heading: Confirming which story applies to you
paragraphs: I pull the Johnson County recorder's lease and deed history for your specific section, then check well status through state records to determine whether you're looking at a dormant CBM interest, active conventional production, or genuinely undeveloped acreage.

faqs.question: My CBM royalty checks stopped years ago. Is my interest worthless?
faqs.answer: No. It has value as a mineral interest even without current production. I'll check the well's plugged status and price it accordingly.

faqs.question: Is coalbed methane still being developed near Buffalo?
faqs.answer: New CBM development has largely stopped basin-wide since prices collapsed. I'll check whether any activity remains on your specific tract.

faqs.question: How is my interest different from conventional oil in the same area?
faqs.answer: CBM and conventional production come from different formations with different decline patterns. I'll identify which applies to your tract before pricing it.
